title: Platform command to a ground station
description:
One command - stream `c` on the relay, platform to station (transport.md). A command is a request, never a guarantee: the platform confirms nothing itself and waits to see the effect in the station's own telemetry. Every command below therefore has a field in a telemetry payload that reports its result - if you add a command, add that field too. Unknown commands must be ignored, not rejected: an older station and a newer platform have to coexist.

The leased commands (radio.audio, video.start) share one shape: the platform repeats the command while the demand exists, a repeat is a renewal rather than a second start, and the lease expiring is the stop signal. Silence has to be the off switch because most consumers never say goodbye - a closed laptop, a dropped link, a crashed platform - and every one of those must stop a station transmitting to nobody on a metered link.

freq_hz.description: Already snapped to the nearest kHz by the platform. Reported back as radio.freq_hz.

db.description: Fixed threshold. Setting one implies leaving AUTO, exactly as moving the slider does on a real receiver. Reported back as radio.threshold_db.

on.description: On: ride 8 dB above the measured floor. Off: FREEZE the threshold where it was - do not keep tracking, or the control appears to do nothing. Reported back as radio.auto_squelch.

Momentary squelch defeat - the MON button. Station-wide: there is one gate, so this pushes hiss to every listener. Expected to be held, never latched.

**The station releases it on its own** after the timeout in transport.md's timings table, and reports monitor false when it does. A console that means to keep it held re-sends before then. Holding the gate open makes squelch_open true, so audio flows continuously up a metered link, and the console holding it can close, crash or be signed out without ever sending the release - the same reason the audio and video leases expire rather than waiting to be told. A station that means to keep it open sends the command again. Reported back as radio.monitor.

gain.description: Site configuration, set once. Prefer fixed: the tuner AGC desenses near strong transmitters badly enough that a stronger signal reads lower. Reported back as radio.gain.

ppm.description: Crystal correction, trimmed once at commissioning. Reported back as radio.ppm.

on.description:
Somebody is looking at the spectrum display, or has stopped. Demand-driven and leased for the same reason as audio and video: a console that crashes stops the traffic without saying goodbye, and the full sweep is tens of megabytes a day on a metered link for a display that is open for minutes at commissioning. Reported back as radio.spectrum and radio.span_hz, present only while asked for.

`false` stops it immediately rather than waiting for the lease, because unlike audio there is no cost to a stop that never arrives - the lease already covers that case.

lease_seconds.description: How long this request is good for. Defaults and bounds are in transport.md's timings table; the station clamps to them.

oneOf.description: Somebody is listening: let audio flow up the link (squelch permitting) for lease_seconds. Repeated while any console holds the audio subscription; a repeat is a renewal. There is no stop command - the lease expiring is the stop signal - and local recording is never gated by this: a transmission nobody had a console open for is still written to disk. Reported back as audio frames on stream `a` while the squelch is open, and as radio.audio_lease_remaining_s.

on.description: Always true. False is deliberately not defined: an unsubscribe-style stop would leave a station transmitting forever when the stopper never arrives, so stopping is the lease's job alone.

lease_seconds.description: How long this request is good for. Defaults and bounds are in transport.md's timings table; the station clamps to them, so an absurd lease cannot pin the uplink open.

oneOf.description:
The first viewer attached: start the live H.264 stream to the media WebSocket (transport.md) and keep it running for lease_seconds. Repeated while anyone is watching; treat a repeat as a renewal, never a second start - there is one camera, and a second encoder on it reads as broken hardware. If the lease expires unrenewed the station stops on its own, so a crashed platform or a dropped link cannot leave it paying for a picture nobody can see. Reported back in health.video.stream.

**No bitrate, resolution or frame rate, deliberately.** The station streams what its camera is configured for and what its link will carry; the platform cannot see either and would be asking for a number it has no way to verify. On-demand plus drop-never-queue is what makes that safe, and health.video.stream reports what was actually achieved. See transport.md.

lease_seconds.description: How long this request is good for. Optional: transport.md's timings table states the default a station applies when the platform names none, and the clamp it applies either way.

viewers.description: How many are watching right now. Advisory and reported straight back in health.video.stream.viewers, so an operator can see that a station is streaming for four people rather than one. It must not change what the station sends: there is one encoder and one stream regardless, and a station that tried to act on this would be optimising for a number it cannot verify.

oneOf.description: The last viewer left. A courtesy that ends the stream sooner than the lease would; the lease expiring remains the guarantee, so a station that never hears this still stops. Reported back in health.video.stream.

reason.description: For the station's log, so 'stopped by the platform' can say why.

oneOf.description:
Somebody is watching this station on a multi-station wall: send a small still every interval_seconds for lease_seconds. Leased exactly like video.start, and for the same reason - silence is the stop signal, so a closed tab cannot leave a station capturing for nobody.

**This is not video, and the difference is the whole point.** A live stream is megabits a second through an in-process relay; a scaled JPEG a minute is a few kilobits and can be served from a cache by any worker. A wall of two dozen stations is affordable in the second form and is a different system in the first.

**The station may refuse, and refusal is not failure.** Unlike every other command here, a station is expected to decline this one on its own authority when its battery is low: a capture is an RTSP handshake, a decode and a JPEG encode, and standing load is what browns a solar site out. It accepts the lease and reports the refusal live in health.video.poster.reason, because the refusal is a condition of the site that can begin and end mid-lease, not a property of the request. The platform must not treat a refusing station as broken.

The still itself goes over HTTP to /media/poster with the station's own credential, not through the relay: the relay carries control and telemetry that must not queue behind bulk data (transport.md). Reported back in health.video.poster.

lease_seconds.description: How long this request is good for. Optional: transport.md's timings table states the default a station applies when the platform names none, and the clamp it applies either way.

interval_seconds.description: How often a still is wanted. A REQUEST, not an instruction: the station floors it at its own minimum and may serve faster if something else on the box (a technician on the setup page) is already driving the camera harder, since one capture serves every watcher. It will never serve slower than asked on purpose.

oneOf.description: Nobody is watching the wall any more. A courtesy that stops the stills sooner than the lease would; the lease expiring remains the guarantee, so a station that never hears this still stops. Reported back in health.video.poster.

reason.description: For the station's log, so 'stopped by the platform' can say why.

oneOf.description: Apply site configuration. Defined so both sides agree on the shape, and currently never sent: the platform holds no site policy of its own, and the settings it does share with the station (position, elevation) must not be editable from two ends - see enrolment.md §7 for when this changes. The station applies what it recognises, persists, and reports back as health.config_version; it never assumes the platform saw the change take.

version.description: The configuration generation this payload represents, echoed back in health.config_version once applied.

config.description: The settings to merge. Keys the station does not know are ignored, not rejected: a newer platform must be able to talk to an older station.

oneOf.description: The platform is finished with every event up to and including through_seq - each one either durably stored or refused as permanently unstorable - so the station may delete them and must not re-send. **The only acknowledgement in this contract**, and it exists because the events channel is the only one carrying facts that have no newer version - everything else is current state and may be dropped. Sent after each batch is durably stored, never on receipt: acknowledging what is still in memory is how a crash silently loses a site's history. A lost ack costs a re-send, which is why events carry a stable id to deduplicate on.

through_seq.description: The highest seq in the batch being acknowledged. The station may delete everything up to and including this and must not re-send it. Read this as 'the batch is dealt with', not as 'the highest row I stored' - a batch whose first event the platform is required to refuse (a reserved `platform.` type, a payload failing this schema) would otherwise have no expressible ack, and the station would re-send it for ever with every later event stuck behind it. A refused event is terminal: re-sending never makes it acceptable, so the cursor moves past it and the platform records the refusal on its own side. See transport.md, Store and forward.

on.description: Reported back as light.on once the hardware has actually done it.

oneOf.description: Update the station to a specific image. Added in 2.1, additive, and like every command ignored by a station that does not know it. The station does NOT update itself: it records this target, and the host-side updater outside its sandbox pulls the pinned digest, verifies its signature, recreates the container, gates on it publishing and rolls back on failure (station DECISIONS.md item 48). Progress is reported as the station's running and desired version in health telemetry, not confirmed here. `digest` is the pin and is required; `tag` is a human label; a station may refuse a malformed target.

image.description: The image repository to pull from (a registry path). Handed to the host updater unchanged.

tag.description: A human-readable version label for the target, echoed back as the desired version. Advisory: the digest is what is pulled and verified.

digest.description: The immutable content digest to pull and run. Required: it is the pin that makes the update tamper-evident, and the signature is checked against it on the box.

force.description: Re-apply a target the station previously rejected. Off by default, so a bad image is not re-pulled every cycle.

oneOf.description: Renew the credential now, and with it adopt the platform's current station record - name and timezone - instead of waiting for the scheduled renewal (enrolment.md §6). Added in 2.1, additive, and ignored by a station that does not know it. Name and timezone are the platform's to set and reach the box only through the enrolment record, so this is how an edit made in the console lands promptly rather than on the next renewal cycle. Position stays the station's own - the platform's copy is only what the station reported - so a renewal round-trips it unchanged. Reported back as the renewed credential expiry in health.credential.
